claim: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has revealed fibrosis in embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS) patients comparable to levels seen in atrial fibrillation (AFib).
source: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has revealed fibrosis in embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS) patients comparable to levels seen in atrial fibrillation (AFib).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior clinical findings, as elaborated in the Introduction section where it references clinical studies.

claim: MRI-based atrial models were reconstructed for 45 ESUS and 45 AFib patients.
source: MRI-based atrial models were reconstructed for 45 ESUS and 45 AFib patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study design and methodology, describing the number of patient-derived models created.

claim: Reentrant drivers were induced in 24/45 (53%) ESUS models.
source: Reentrant drivers were induced in 24/45 (53%) ESUS and 22/45 (49%) AFib models.
evidence: This is a direct report of simulation results showing the number and percentage of ESUS models in which reentrant drivers were induced.

claim: Reentrant drivers were induced in 22/45 (49%) AFib models.
source: Reentrant drivers were induced in 24/45 (53%) ESUS and 22/45 (49%) AFib models.
evidence: This is a direct report of simulation results showing the number and percentage of AFib models in which reentrant drivers were induced.

claim: Inducible models had more fibrosis (16.7 ± 5.45%) than non-inducible models (11.07 ± 3.61%; p<0.0001).
source: Inducible models had more fibrosis (16.7 ± 5.45%) than non-inducible models (11.07 ± 3.61%; p<0.0001)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the simulations with statistical significance testing.

claim: Inducible subsets of ESUS and AFib models had similar fibrosis levels (p=0.90).
source: however, inducible subsets of ESUS and AFib models had similar fibrosis levels (p=0.90)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of fibrosis levels between inducible ESUS and AFib models.

claim: The intrinsic pro-arrhythmic substrate properties of fibrosis in ESUS and AFib are indistinguishable.
source: meaning that the intrinsic pro-arrhythmic substrate properties of fibrosis in ESUS and AFib are indistinguishable.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical finding that inducible ESUS and AFib models have similar fibrosis levels.

claim: Some ESUS patients have latent pre-clinical fibrotic substrate that could be a future source of arrhythmogenicity.
source: This suggests that some ESUS patients have latent pre-clinical fibrotic substrate that could be a future source of arrhythmogenicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results showing that ESUS models can sustain reentrant drivers.

claim: ESUS patients with fibrotic atria are spared from AFib due to an absence of arrhythmia triggers.
source: Thus, our work prompts the hypothesis that ESUS patients with fibrotic atria are spared from AFib due to an absence of arrhythmia triggers.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis prompted by the study findings.

claim: Atrial fibrillation (AFib) affects 1–2% of the world's population.
source: Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is the most common cardiac arrhythmia, affecting 1–2% of the world's population and significantly contributing to worldwide morbidity and mortality (Andrade et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Andrade et al., 2014.

claim: Around 20% of all ischemic strokes occur in AFib patients.
source: The primary source of AFib-related mortality is stroke, with around 20% of all ischemic strokes occurring in AFib patients (Andrade et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Andrade et al., 2014.

claim: Sub-clinical AFib is implicated as a potential cause of embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS).
source: Sub-clinical AFib (i.e., transient, asymptomatic AFib) is implicated as a potential cause of embolic stroke of undetermined source (ESUS)
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge in the field.

claim: AFib has been detected in only 30% of patients with long-term rhythm monitoring following ESUS.
source: Clinical studies have shown that AFib has been detected in only 30% of patients with long-term rhythm monitoring (Brachmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brachmann et al., 2016.

claim: The left atrial fibrosis burden measured by late gadolinium enhanced-magnetic resonance imaging (LGE-MRI) is as high in ESUS patients as in AFib patients without stroke.
source: Recent evidence from clinical studies suggests that the left atrial fibrosis burden measured by late gadolinium enhanced-magnetic resonance imaging (LGE-MRI) is as high in ESUS patients as in AFib patients without stroke (Tandon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tandon et al., 2019.

claim: Atrial fibrosis is an element of the causal pathway for stroke, through an atrial cardiopathy, and independent of AFib.
source: This finding supports the hypothesis that atrial fibrosis is an element of the causal pathway for stroke, through an atrial cardiopathy, and independent of AFib.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by the clinical finding about fibrosis levels in ESUS.

claim: Personalized atrial models have been used to assess arrhythmogenic propensity of fibrotic substrate and predict AFib ablation targets.
source: Previously, personalized atrial models have been used to assess arrhythmogenic propensity of fibrotic substrate and predict AFib ablation targets (Zahid et al., 2016a; Boyle et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zahid et al., 2016a and Boyle et al., 2019.

claim: Ninety patient-derived models were included in the analysis: 45 post-stroke ESUS and 45 pre-ablation AFib patients.
source: Ninety patient-derived models were included in our analysis: 45 post-stroke ESUS and 45 pre-ablation AFib patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study cohort size and composition.

claim: There was a significant difference in left atrial (LA) surface area between ESUS and AFib patients.
source: There was a significant difference in left atrial (LA) surface area
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing LA surface area values and p-value.

claim: LA volume index was not significantly different between ESUS and AFib patients.
source: the lack of difference in LA volume index (a more commonly used measurement of normalized LA surface area)
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 showing p=0.607 for LA volume index.

claim: LA fibrosis burden was not significantly different between ESUS (13.6 ± 6.2%) and AFib patients (14.2 ± 4.5%) (p=0.91).
source: LA fibrosis burden was not significantly different between ESUS (13.6 ± 6.2%) and AFib patients (14.2 ± 4.5%) (p=0.91), consistent with previous findings (Tandon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and statistical testing, with citation to Tandon et al., 2019 for consistency with prior findings.

claim: The capability of the fibrotic substrate to sustain RDs was not significantly different between ESUS and AFib groups (p=0.83).
source: Thus, the capability of the fibrotic substrate to sustain RDs was not significantly different between the two groups (p=0.83, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and statistical testing, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: For models in the first quartile (fibrosis < 9.75%), 21.7% showed at least one pacing site that induced RD-sustained arrhythmia.
source: For five models (21.7%) in the first quartile (fibrosis < 9.75%), six models (28.5%) in the second quartile (fibrosis < 12.6%), 15 (62.5%) models in the third quartile (fibrosis < 17. 5%), and 20 (91.0%) models in the top quartile, simulations revealed at least one pacing site for which stimulation produced an episode of RD-sustained arrhythmia (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results organized by fibrosis quartiles, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: For models in the second quartile (fibrosis < 12.6%), 28.5% showed at least one pacing site that induced RD-sustained arrhythmia.
source: For five models (21.7%) in the first quartile (fibrosis < 9.75%), six models (28.5%) in the second quartile (fibrosis < 12.6%), 15 (62.5%) models in the third quartile (fibrosis < 17. 5%), and 20 (91.0%) models in the top quartile, simulations revealed at least one pacing site for which stimulation produced an episode of RD-sustained arrhythmia (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results organized by fibrosis quartiles, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: For models in the third quartile (fibrosis < 17.5%), 62.5% showed at least one pacing site that induced RD-sustained arrhythmia.
source: For five models (21.7%) in the first quartile (fibrosis < 9.75%), six models (28.5%) in the second quartile (fibrosis < 12.6%), 15 (62.5%) models in the third quartile (fibrosis < 17. 5%), and 20 (91.0%) models in the top quartile, simulations revealed at least one pacing site for which stimulation produced an episode of RD-sustained arrhythmia (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results organized by fibrosis quartiles, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: For models in the top quartile of fibrosis, 91.0% showed at least one pacing site that induced RD-sustained arrhythmia.
source: For five models (21.7%) in the first quartile (fibrosis < 9.75%), six models (28.5%) in the second quartile (fibrosis < 12.6%), 15 (62.5%) models in the third quartile (fibrosis < 17. 5%), and 20 (91.0%) models in the top quartile, simulations revealed at least one pacing site for which stimulation produced an episode of RD-sustained arrhythmia (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results organized by fibrosis quartiles, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Fibrosis burden was not significantly different between inducible ESUS and AFib models (p=0.90, CI: [−3.4, 4.1]).
source: Fibrosis burden was not significantly different between inducible ESUS and AFib models with (Figure 3A; p=0.90, confidence interval; CI: [−3.4, 4.1])
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of fibrosis levels in inducible models, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Fibrosis burden was not significantly different between non-inducible ESUS and AFib models (p=1, CI: [−2.1, 2.4]).
source: or without induced reentry (Figure 3A; p=1, CI: [−2.1, 2.4]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of fibrosis levels in non-inducible models, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: When fibrosis burdens for inducible and non-inducible models were aggregated across ESUS and AFib groups, a significant difference was evident (16.7 ± 5.46% vs. 11.07 ± 3.61%; p<0.0001, CI: [3.4, 7.6]).
source: However, when fibrosis burdens for inducible and non-inducible models were aggregated across ESUS and AFib groups, a significant difference was evident (Figure 3A; 16.7 ± 5.46% vs. 11.07 ± 3.61%; p<0.0001, CI: [3.4, 7.6]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of aggregated fibrosis data, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The median number of unique RDs was one for both AFib and ESUS models.
source: In all 46 inducible models, the median number of unique RDs was one for both AFib and ESUS models (AFib range: 1–5; ESUS range: 1–8).
evidence: This is a direct report of simulation results for unique RD counts.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of unique reentrant morphologies per model between AFib and ESUS groups (p=0.83, CI: [−7.7 × 10−5, 8.8 × 10−5]).
source: There was no significant difference in the number of unique reentrant morphologies per model between the two groups (Figure 3B; p=0.83, CI: [−7.7 × 10−5, 8.8 × 10−5]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The number of unique RDs was positively correlated with atrial fibrosis burden (R = 0.63, p<0.0001).
source: The number of unique RDs was positively correlated with atrial fibrosis burden (Figure 3C; R = 0.63, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The median number of stimulation sites from which rapid pacing led to RD formation was three for AFib and two for ESUS models.
source: For all RD-inducible cases, the median number of stimulation sites from which rapid pacing led to RD formation was three for AFib and two for ESUS models (range for both groups: 1–9).
evidence: This is a direct report of simulation results for pacing site counts.

claim: No significant difference was found in the number of pacing sites that induced reentry per model between AFib and ESUS (p=0.79, CI: [−2.0, 1.0]).
source: No significant difference was found in the number of pacing sites that induced reentry per model between AFib and ESUS (Figure 3D; p=0.79, CI: [−2.0, 1.0]).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The number of RD inducing pacing sites was significantly correlated with fibrosis burden (R = 0.62, p<0.0001).
source: The number of RD inducing pacing sites was also significantly correlated with fibrosis burden (Figure 3E; R = 0.62, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Fibrosis may directly lead to increased AFib trigger incidence via calcium dysregulation leading to localized regions of depolarized resting potential.
source: In addition to its role as part of the substrate for reentrant arrhythmia, fibrosis may directly lead to increased AFib trigger incidence via calcium dysregulation leading to localized to regions of depolarized resting potential (Gouvêa de Barros et al., 2015; Alonso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gouvêa de Barros et al., 2015 and Alonso et al., 2016.

claim: No significant difference was found in the extent of abnormally depolarized tissue between ESUS and AFib models (p=0.32; CI: [–0.007, 0.019]).
source: We found no significant difference in these values between ESUS and AFib models (Figure 3F; p=0.32; CI: [–0.007, 0.019])
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and statistical testing, with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: There was a trend toward more trigger-prone tissue in ESUS compared to AFib.
source: if anything, there was a trend toward more trigger-prone tissue in ESUS.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, though not statistically significant.

claim: Analysis of simulated reentry episodes revealed no qualitative differences in arrhythmia dynamics between AFib and ESUS models.
source: Analysis of simulated reentry episodes revealed no qualitative differences in arrhythmia dynamics between AFib and ESUS models.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the qualitative analysis of simulation results.

claim: Both ESUS and AFib models exhibited activation patterns consistent with previous definitions of RD-driven arrhythmia.
source: Overall, this shows that both ESUS and AFib models exhibited activation patterns consistent with previous definitions of RD-driven arrhythmia
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing simulation results to established definitions in the literature.

claim: Fibrosis burden alone is an insufficient predictor for a potential arrhythmic substrate.
source: examples of inducible low-fibrosis and non-inducible high-fibrosis models emphasize that fibrosis burden alone is an insufficient predictor for a potential arrhythmic substrate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of outlier cases in the simulation results.

claim: ESUS and AFib models had a statistically similar pattern of inducibility rates (p=0.45, by χ2 test).
source: While ESUS and AFib models had a statistically similar pattern of inducibility rates (p=0.45, by χ2 test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of regional inducibility patterns.

claim: Stimulation from the posterior wall was approximately two times more likely to induce RDs in AFib models than ESUS models (IdS = 6 vs. IdS = 3).
source: stimulation from the posterior wall was approximately two times more likely to induce RDs in AFib models than ESUS models (Figure 5A, IdS = 6 vs. IdS = 3).
evidence: This is supported by inducibility score analysis with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The LPV region was most likely to harbor RDs in the AFib cohort (N = 17).
source: The LPV region was most likely to harbor RDs in the AFib cohort (Figure 5C, N = 17).
evidence: This is supported by RD localization analysis with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: In the ESUS cohort, the anterior wall was the most likely region to contain an RD (N = 16).
source: In the ESUS cohort, the anterior wall was the most likely region to contain an RD (Figure 5D, N = 16).
evidence: This is supported by RD localization analysis with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The association between the type of model (ESUS vs. AFib) and RD localization was not significant (p=0.13, χ2 test).
source: The association between the type of model (ESUS vs. AFib) and RD localization was not significant (p=0.13, χ2 test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of RD localization patterns.

claim: Fibrotic tissue areas with both high local fibrosis density (FD) and high local fibrosis entropy (FE) have increased propensity for RD localization.
source: Fibrotic tissue areas with both high local fibrosis density (FD) and high local fibrosis entropy (FE) have increased propensity for RD localization, as shown in computational models (Roney et al., 2016) and intracardiac mapping of patients with persistent AFib (Cochet et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roney et al., 2016 and Cochet et al., 2018.

claim: The extent of pro-RD tissue in the LPV region was significantly higher in AFib compared to ESUS models (p=0.01).
source: This analysis revealed that the extent of pro-RD tissue in the LPV region was significantly higher in AFib compared to ESUS models (Figure 6B; p=0.01)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of fibrosis spatial patterns with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: This is the first study to use computational modeling and simulation to assess potential pro-arrhythmic capacity of LA fibrosis in ESUS patients.
source: This is the first study to use computational modeling and simulation to assess potential pro-arrhythmic capacity of LA fibrosis in ESUS patients.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study approach.

claim: This is the largest cohort ever studied via computational analysis of atrial electrophysiology in models derived from LGE-MRI, exceeding the number of patient-specific models (N = 50) in the former largest study by a factor of ≈1.8.
source: Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, this is the largest cohort ever studied via computational analysis of atrial electrophysiology in models derived from LGE-MRI, exceeding the number of patient-specific models (N = 50) in the former largest study (Roney et al., 2020) by a factor of ≈1.8.
evidence: This is a claim about the study size relative to prior work, with citation to Roney et al., 2020.

claim: Atrial fibrosis results in changes that promote reentry.
source: Experimental findings have shown that atrial fibrosis results in changes that promote reentry (Xia et al., 2004; Litchenberg et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xia et al., 2004 and Litchenberg et al., 2000.

claim: The exact mechanism of the connection between atrial fibrosis and reentry is not fully understood.
source: but the exact mechanism of this connection is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Previous modeling studies have linked RD localization to specific spatial patterns of fibrotic remodeling in AFib.
source: Previous modeling studies have linked RD localization to specific spatial patterns of fibrotic remodeling in AFib (Zahid et al., 2016a; Hakim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zahid et al., 2016a and Hakim et al., 2018.

claim: Atrial fibrosis burden does not differ significantly between AFib and ESUS patients.
source: Recent clinical findings indicate that atrial fibrosis burden does not differ significantly between AFib and ESUS patients
evidence: This is stated as a recent clinical finding, consistent with the study's own data.

claim: ESUS patients do not demonstrate AFib at the time of stroke or during ambulatory monitoring.
source: and yet (by definition) ESUS patients do not demonstrate AFib at the time of stroke or during ambulatory monitoring (Tandon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as part of the definition of ESUS, with citation to Tandon et al., 2019.

claim: Fibrotic substrate in individuals with ESUS is indistinguishable from that in patients with AFib in terms of the fundamental capacity to sustain RDs.
source: From the standpoint of computational models derived from patient LGE-MRI scans, fibrotic substrate in individuals with ESUS is indistinguishable from that in patients with AFib in terms of the fundamental capacity to sustain RDs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: For inducible models from both cohorts, high fibrosis models were more likely to exhibit RDs irrespective of whether they corresponded to ESUS or AFib patients.
source: For inducible models from both cohorts, we found that high fibrosis models were more likely to exhibit RDs irrespective of whether they corresponded to ESUS or AFib patients.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation data analysis.

claim: This finding is in agreement with prior computational studies, which found the same general association between fibrosis and RDs.
source: This is in agreement with prior computational studies, which found the same general association (Zahid et al., 2016a; Boyle et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zahid et al., 2016a and Boyle et al., 2019.

claim: Higher fibrosis burden is associated with poor outcomes in AFib ablation procedures.
source: and is consistent with clinical understanding, wherein higher fibrosis burden is associated with poor outcomes in AFib ablation procedures (Marrouche et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marrouche et al., 2014.

claim: Assessment of raw fibrosis burden from LGE-MRI scans alone is insufficient to fully characterize arrhythmogenic capacity of potentially pro-arrhythmic substrate in ESUS.
source: This observation confirms that, as observed previously in analogous AFib modeling studies (Zahid et al., 2016a; Boyle et al., 2019), assessment of raw fibrosis burden LGE-MRI scans alone is insufficient to fully characterize arrhythmogenic capacity of potentially pro-arrhythmic substrate in ESUS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of outlier cases, with citations to prior studies.

claim: The potential for fibrosis itself to serve as a source of arrhythmia triggers is no greater in AFib than in ESUS models.
source: Additionally, our analysis of abnormal steady-state depolarization in LA models suggests the potential for fibrosis itself to serve as a source of arrhythmia triggers is no greater in AFib than in ESUS models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of depolarized tissue in simulations.

claim: The rate of inducibility in this study (22 of 45 AFib models) is consistent with previous studies (e.g., 13 of 20 in computational models reconstructed from LGE-MRI scans of persistent AFib patients).
source: This rate of inducibility is consistent with previous studies (e.g., 13 of 20 in computational models reconstructed from LGE-MRI scans of persistent AFib patients) (Zahid et al., 2016a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zahid et al., 2016a.

claim: LA fibrosis is associated with increased arrhythmia inducibility but fails to tell the whole story.
source: supporting the notion that LA fibrosis is associated with increased arrhythmia inducibility but fails to tell the whole story.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inducibility results and comparison to prior studies.

claim: There is no difference between ESUS and AFib patients in terms of the fundamental capacity of the fibrotic substrate to potentially harbor RDs.
source: Importantly, neither of these model constraints repudiates the central finding of our study, which suggests that there is no difference between ESUS and AFib patients in terms of the fundamental capacity of the fibrotic substrate to potentially harbor RDs.
evidence: This is a restatement of the central finding of the study.

claim: There was no significant difference in global fibrosis burden between inducible AFib and ESUS models.
source: First, we found that there was no significant difference in global fibrosis burden between inducible AFib and ESUS models.
evidence: This is a restatement of a key finding from the results section.

claim: Intrinsic pro-arrhythmic traits of ESUS and AFib fibrotic substrate are indistinguishable.
source: Thus, our computational modeling suggests that intrinsic pro-arrhythmic traits of ESUS and AFib fibrotic substrate are indistinguishable.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fibrosis burden comparison.

claim: One potential alternative explanation for the lack of arrhythmia in ESUS patients is a lack of suitable triggers, despite an abundance of fibrotic substrate on par with that observed in AFib.
source: Given this result, one potential alternative explanation for the lack of arrhythmia in ESUS patients is a lack of suitable triggers, despite an abundance of fibrotic substrate on par with that observed in AFib.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the simulation findings.

claim: The pacing sites used in this study were based on common AFib trigger sites as identified in a recent clinical study.
source: The plausibility of this explanation is strengthened by the fact that the pacing sites from which episodes of reentry were induced in our study were based on common AFib trigger sites as identified in a recent clinical study (Santangeli and Marchlinski, 2017)
evidence: This is a description of the study methodology with citation to Santangeli and Marchlinski, 2017.

claim: In more than half of the ESUS cohort (24/45), if the atria were subjected to the same type of triggered activity known to occur in typical AFib patients, the result could be sustained arrhythmia.
source: In more than half of the cohort (24/45), our analysis suggests that the answer is yes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results showing inducibility in 24/45 ESUS models.

claim: There was no difference in the number of unique model-predicted RDs or the number of pacing sites that induced RDs between ESUS and AFib.
source: Specifically, we found no difference in the number of unique model-predicted RDs or the number of pacing sites that induced RDs between ESUS and AFib.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the results section.

claim: The number of unique RDs and the number of pacing sites that induced RDs were highly correlated with LA fibrosis burden.
source: Instead, these variables were highly correlated with LA fibrosis burden
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis in the results section.

claim: High fibrosis models are more susceptible to pacing-induced RDs.
source: which is consistent with the concept that high fibrosis models are more susceptible to pacing-induced RDs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: In the presence of simulated triggered activity, both the substrate's capacity to sustain reentry and its susceptibility to triggered activity are closely linked to global fibrosis burden.
source: The general implication is that in the presence of simulated triggered activity, both of these characteristics are closely linked to global fibrosis burden.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the correlation findings.

claim: RDs identified by non-invasive electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) and in silico phase singularity identification have been shown to co-localize with fibrosis boundary zones identified by LGE-MRI.
source: RDs identified by non-invasive electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) and in silico phase singularity identification have been shown to co-localize with fibrosis boundary zones identified by LGE-MRI (Zahid et al., 2016a; Roney et al., 2016; Boyle et al., 2018a; Cochet et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: RD localization dynamics in this study were consistent with findings that RDs co-localize with fibrosis boundary zones.
source: RD localization dynamics in this study were consistent with these findings, as illustrated by representative LA fibrotic tissue distributions and corresponding RDs in Figure 4.
evidence: This is a statement of consistency between the current study and prior findings, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: RD morphology in this study corroborated previous findings – arrhythmias were perpetuated by one RD at a time, with activity in the periphery including conduction block, transient reentry, and wavefront collision.
source: RD morphology in this study corroborated previous findings – arrhythmias were perpetuated by one RD at a time, with activity in the periphery including conduction block, transient reentry, and wavefront collision (Zahid et al., 2016a; Boyle et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement of consistency with prior studies, with citations to Zahid et al., 2016a and Boyle et al., 2019.

claim: Spatial properties of the fibrotic substrate between AFib and ESUS models are not intrinsically different.
source: Further to the macroscopic analysis discussed above, our region-by-region analysis of RD inducibility and localization showed that spatial properties of the fibrotic substrate between AFib and ESUS models are not intrinsically different.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regional analysis.

claim: The IdS score for the posterior wall region was ≈2× higher in AFib compared to ESUS models.
source: The most striking difference exists for the posterior wall region, where the IdS score was ≈2× higher in AFib compared to ESUS models.
evidence: This is a finding from the regional inducibility analysis.

claim: Even in cases where posterior LA wall ectopic excitations occur in ESUS patients, simulations suggest that they could be up to 50% less likely to engage the fibrotic substrate and initiate sustained reentry compared to the same activity in AFib patients.
source: Thus, even in cases where posterior LA wall ectopic excitations occur in ESUS patients, our simulations suggest that they could be up to 50% less likely to engage the fibrotic substrate and initiate sustained reentry compared to the same activity in AFib patients.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the IdS score difference in the posterior wall region.

claim: Evidence from ECGI mapping indicates that reentrant activity occurs most frequently in the PV and posterior wall regions.
source: While understanding of RD localization dynamics in AFib remains limited, evidence from ECGI mapping indicates that reentrant activity occurs most frequently in the PV and posterior wall regions (Boyle et al., 2018a; Haissaguerre et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The study findings are consistent with ECGI data for AFib but not ESUS models.
source: Our findings are consistent with these data for AFib but not ESUS models.
evidence: This is a comparison of the study findings to prior ECGI data.

claim: Many (41.1%) AFib model RDs localized to the LPV region.
source: Many (41.1%) AFib model RDs localized to the LPV region.
evidence: This is a finding from the RD localization analysis.

claim: In the ESUS population the RD localization hotspot was the region comprising the anterior wall and LAA (37%).
source: In contrast, in the ESUS population the RD localization hotspot was the region comprising the anterior wall and LAA (37%).
evidence: This is a finding from the RD localization analysis.

claim: The proportion of tissue with the propensity to harbor RDs was higher in the LPV region for AFib compared to ESUS models.
source: Finally, our analysis of fibrosis spatial patterns revealed that the proportion of tissue with the propensity to harbor RDs (as established via machine learning in prior work Zahid et al., 2016a) was higher in the LPV region for AFib compared to ESUS models.
evidence: This is a finding from the pro-RD tissue analysis, with citation to Zahid et al., 2016a.

claim: ESUS patients trended toward a higher percentage of pro-RD tissue in all anatomical areas except the LPVs.
source: In contrast, ESUS patients trended toward a higher percentage of pro-RD tissue in all anatomical areas except the LPVs.

claim: If the ESUS substrate were subjected to suitable triggered activity, it could sustain the same types of RDs as those that contribute to AFib perpetuation.
source: Thus, despite some interesting and potentially consequential differences in regional distribution of potentially pro-arrhythmic fibrosis, our overarching conclusion remains unchanged: our models suggest that if the ESUS substrate were subjected to suitable triggered activity, it could sustain the same types of RDs as those that contribute to AFib perpetuation.

claim: Atrial tissue is modeled as a bilayer to drastically reduce computational load.
source: In this study, atrial tissue is modeled as a bilayer to drastically reduce computational load.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Previous studies have used the bilayer modeling framework to represent human atria effectively.
source: Previous studies have used this modeling framework (Roney et al., 2016; Labarthe et al., 2014) to represent human atria effectively
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roney et al., 2016 and Labarthe et al., 2014.

claim: The bilayer framework remains a simplification compared to volumetric 3D models.
source: but the framework remains a simplification compared to volumetric 3D models.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the modeling approach.

claim: Clinical-grade MRI resolution limits the ability to detect fine details in anatomical structure and spatial distribution of potentially arrhythmogenic substrate.
source: Moreover, clinical-grade MRI resolution limits our ability to detect fine details in anatomical structure and spatial distribution of potentially arrhythmogenic substrate, for instance slow-conducting tracks of fibrotic atrial tissue that could underlie microreentrant circuits (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation with citation to Hansen et al., 2018.

claim: The models do not incorporate inter-patient variability in conduction velocity (CV) and electrophysiological properties such as ion channel expression.
source: While these models are patient-specific in terms of LA anatomy and each individual's unique pattern of fibrotic remodeling, they do not incorporate inter-patient variability in conduction velocity (CV) and electrophysiological properties such as ion channel expression.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the modeling approach.

claim: Previous analysis indicates that the representation of atrial architecture with generic 'average AFib' electrophysiology is appropriate for use in patient-derived modeling.
source: Nevertheless, our previous analysis indicates that this representation of atrial architecture with generic 'average AFib' electrophysiology is appropriate for use in patient-derived modeling (Hakim et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hakim et al., 2018 and Deng et al., 2017.

claim: The models do not differentiate between cell- or tissue-scale properties of atrial electrophysiology between patients with paroxysmal and persistent forms of AFib.
source: As in previous studies (Ali et al., 2019; Shade et al., 2020), our models do not differentiate between cell- or tissue-scale properties of atrial electrophysiology between patients with paroxysmal and persistent forms of AFib.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation with citations to Ali et al., 2019 and Shade et al., 2020.

claim: The approach to characterizing potential arrhythmia propensity in ESUS patients assumes cell- and tissue-scale remodeling based on experimental and clinical data from the AFib milieu.
source: Likewise, our approach to characterizing potential arrhythmia propensity in ESUS patients assumes cell- and tissue-scale remodeling based on experimental and clinical data from the AFib milieu.
evidence: This is a description of an assumption in the modeling approach.

claim: The modeling and simulation methodology allows assessment of whether there are any relevant differences in the spatial pattern of fibrotic remodeling between ESUS and AFib patients in the absence of other potentially confounding variables.
source: Specifically, it allows us to assess whether there are any relevant differences in the spatial pattern of fibrotic remodeling between ESUS and AFib patients in the absence of other potentially confounding variables.
evidence: This is a description of an advantage of the modeling approach.

claim: Patients with stroke were excluded from the AFib cohort.
source: A related limitation is that patients with stroke were excluded from the AFib cohort.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: Stroke etiology in the database from which AFib patients were drawn was not explicitly adjudicated to be cardioembolic, other ischemic such as atherosclerotic, or hemorrhagic.
source: This was because stroke etiology in the database from which AFib patients were drawn was not explicitly adjudicated to be cardioembolic, other ischemic such as atherosclerotic, or hemorrhagic.
evidence: This is an explanation for the exclusion of stroke patients from the AFib cohort.

claim: The mechanism of stroke in ESUS patients may be independent of AFib.
source: Finally, the mechanism of stroke in ESUS patients may be independent of AFib.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of an alternative explanation.

claim: Decreased atrial function due to atrial fibrosis may contribute to reduced hemodynamic efficacy and thrombus formation in the absence of AFib.
source: Decreased atrial function due to atrial fibrosis may contribute to reduced hemodynamic efficacy and thrombus formation in the absence of AFib.
evidence: This is a speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: Secondary stroke prophylaxis is currently dependent on detecting AFib.
source: Currently, secondary stroke prophylaxis is dependent on detecting AFib
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice.

claim: Predicting through computational modeling which atria are more prone to manifest AFib may be of clinical value.
source: and predicting, through computational modeling, which atria are more prone to manifest AFib may be of clinical value.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: Simulations suggest that the pro-arrhythmic properties of fibrotic substrate in ESUS and AFib patients are indistinguishable.
source: Simulations suggest that the pro-arrhythmic properties of fibrotic substrate in ESUS and AFib patients are indistinguishable.
evidence: This is a restatement of the main conclusion.

claim: Fibrotic remodeling in ESUS patients has the theoretical capacity to sustain reentry when subjected to common AFib triggers.
source: Our results show that fibrotic remodeling in ESUS patients has the theoretical capacity to sustain reentry when subjected to common AFib triggers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Fibrotic substrate conducive to perpetuating reentry may exist in up to half of ESUS patients.
source: Thus, we conclude that fibrotic substrate conducive to perpetuating reentry may exist in up to half of ESUS patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that 24/45 ESUS models were inducible.

claim: The findings support the notion that the lack of AFib in ESUS patients may be attributable to a lack of suitable arrhythmic triggers.
source: Our findings also support the notion that the lack of AFib in this population may be attributable to a lack of suitable arrhythmic triggers, but further research is needed to fully justify this claim.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the findings, with acknowledgment that further research is needed.

claim: While the existence of pre-clinical substrate is correlated with a higher global proportion of fibrotic tissue, many ESUS cases defied these expectations.
source: While the existence of pre-clinical substrate is correlated with a higher global proportion of fibrotic tissue, many ESUS cases defied these expectations
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of outlier cases.

claim: Fibrosis burden alone is insufficient for predicting pre-clinical AFib substrate.
source: suggesting that fibrosis burden alone is insufficient for predicting pre-clinical AFib substrate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of outlier cases.

claim: This conclusion justifies the use of computational simulations to probe beyond the fibrosis as imaged.
source: This conclusion justifies the use of computational simulations to probe beyond the fibrosis as imaged.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the computational approach.

claim: These results provide novel insights into the role of atrial fibrotic remodeling as a critical nexus between the otherwise distinct manifestations of AFib and ESUS.
source: Overall, these results provide novel insights into the role of atrial fibrotic remodeling as a critical nexus between the otherwise distinct manifestations of AFib and ESUS.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: Patients were recruited from the University of Washington (Seattle, WA) and Klinikum Coburg (Coburg, Germany) between July 2016 and June 2019.
source: Patients were recruited to undergo cardiac LGE-MRI from the University of Washington (Seattle, WA) and Klinikum Coburg (Coburg, Germany) between July 2016 and June 2019.
evidence: This is a description of the patient recruitment.

claim: Patients with ESUS met published diagnostic criteria.
source: Patients with ESUS met published diagnostic criteria (Hart et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of patient selection criteria with citation to Hart et al., 2017.

claim: 60% (27/45) of AFib patients had paroxysmal AFib.
source: Patients with paroxysmal (27/45, 60%) or persistent AFib and without stroke were recruited from the UW Cardiac Arrhythmia Data Repository
evidence: This is a description of the AFib patient cohort composition.

claim: Cardiac LGE-MRI was obtained on all participants to quantify the extent of LA fibrosis using previously described protocols.
source: Cardiac LGE-MRI was obtained on all participants to quantify the extent of LA fibrosis using previously described protocols (Marrouche et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the imaging protocol with citation to Marrouche et al., 2014.

claim: Scans were performed on Philips Ingenia and Siemens Avanto clinical scanners.
source: Scans were performed on Philips Ingenia and Siemens Avanto clinical scanners
evidence: This is a description of the imaging equipment used.

claim: Acquisition parameters included transverse imaging volume with a voxel size of 1.25 × 1.25 × 2.5 mm (reconstructed to 0.625 × 0.625 × 1.25 mm).
source: Acquisition parameters included transverse imaging volume with a voxel size of 1.25 × 1.25 × 2.5 mm (reconstructed to 0.625 × 0.625 × 1.25 mm).
evidence: This is a description of the imaging parameters.

claim: Geometric models were reconstructed from LGE-MRI, and the relative extent of fibrosis in the LA was quantified via an adaptive histogram thresholding algorithm.
source: Geometric models were reconstructed from LGE-MRI, and the relative extent of fibrosis in the LA was quantified via an adaptive histogram thresholding algorithm (Jadidi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the model reconstruction process with citation to Jadidi et al., 2013.

claim: Clinical-grade meshes produced by Merisight Inc were resampled with a target resolution of 200 µm using an automated process based on gmsh.
source: Clinical-grade meshes (i.e., coarse discretization) produced by Merisight Inc (Salt Lake City, UT) were resampled with a target resolution of 200 µm using an automated process based on gmsh (Geuzaine and Remacle, 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the mesh processing with citation to Geuzaine and Remacle, 2009.

claim: Each LA model was represented as a bilayer comprising of nested endocardial and epicardial shells, linked at every point by linear connections (σ = 0.8 S m−1).
source: Each LA model was represented as a bilayer comprising of nested endocardial and epicardial shells (Labarthe et al., 2014), linked at every point by linear connections (σ = 0.8 S m−1) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure with citation to Labarthe et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Realistic myocardial fiber orientations were mapped from an atlas geometry using the universal atrial coordinates (UAC) approach.
source: In each patient-derived model, realistic myocardial fiber orientations were mapped from an atlas geometry (Labarthe et al., 2014) using the universal atrial coordinates (UAC) approach.
evidence: This is a description of the fiber mapping process with citation to Labarthe et al., 2014.

claim: In all finite-element LA meshes, the average element edge length was ≈188 µm and the number of nodes ranged from ≈600,000 to ≈1.4 million, depending on LA size.
source: In all finite-element LA meshes, the average element edge length was ≈188 µm and the number of nodes ranged from ≈600,000 to ≈1.4 million, depending on LA size.
evidence: This is a description of the mesh characteristics.

claim: This mesh resolution is consistent with previously established benchmarks for minimizing numerical error due to spatial discretization in simulations of cardiac wavefront propagation.
source: This mesh resolution is consistent with previously established benchmarks for minimizing numerical error due to spatial discretization in simulations of cardiac wavefront propagation (Niederer et al., 2011; Boyle et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Niederer et al., 2011 and Boyle et al., 2021b.

claim: In non-fibrotic regions, a human atrial action potential model was used to represent membrane kinetics, including parameter modifications to fit clinical monophasic action potential recordings from AFib patients.
source: Briefly, in non-fibrotic regions, a human atrial action potential model (Courtemanche et al., 1998) was used to represent membrane kinetics, including parameter modifications to fit clinical monophasic action potential recordings from AFib patients (IKur, Ito, and ICaL decreased by 50%, 50%, and 70%, respectively) (Zahid et al., 2016a; Krummen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the electrophysiology model with citations to Courtemanche et al., 1998, Zahid et al., 2016a, and Krummen et al., 2012.

claim: Conductivity tensor values in non-fibrotic tissue were calibrated to obtain effective CV values of 71.49 cm s−1 and 37.14 cm s−1 (longitudinal and transverse).
source: At the tissue scale, conductivity tensor values in non-fibrotic tissue (longitudinal: σL = 0.409 S m−1; transverse: σT = 0.0820 S m−1) were calibrated to obtain effective CV values of 71.49 cm s−1 and 37.14 cm s−1 (longitudinal and transverse).
evidence: This is a description of the tissue-scale parameters.

claim: In fibrotic regions, modifications to the AFib-like action potential model (ICaL, INa, and IK1 decreased by 50%, 40%, and 50%, respectively) were implemented as in prior studies.
source: In fibrotic regions, modifications to the AFib-like action potential model (ICaL, INa, and IK1 decreased by 50%, 40%, and 50%, respectively) were implemented as in prior studies (Zahid et al., 2016a; Zahid et al., 2016b)
evidence: This is a description of the fibrotic tissue model with citations to Zahid et al., 2016a and Zahid et al., 2016b.

claim: These changes resulted in a 15.4% increase in action potential duration and a 49.6% decrease in upstroke velocity.
source: resulting in a 15.4% increase in action potential duration and a 49.6% decrease in upstroke velocity.
evidence: This is a description of the effects of the fibrotic tissue model parameters.

claim: Tissue-scale effects of interstitial fibrosis and gap junction remodeling were represented by reducing overall conductivity and exaggerating the anisotropy ratio (σL:σT) from 5:1 to 8:1.
source: As in previous studies (Zahid et al., 2016a; Boyle et al., 2018a; Boyle et al., 2018b), tissue-scale effects of interstitial fibrosis and gap junction remodeling were represented by reducing overall conductivity and exaggerating the anisotropy ratio (σL:σT) from 5:1 to 8:1 (σL = 0.177 S m−1; σT = 0.0221 S m−1).
evidence: This is a description of the tissue-scale fibrosis model with citations to prior studies.

claim: Electrical propagation in bilayer LA models was simulated by solving the monodomain equation using the finite-element method.
source: Electrical propagation in bilayer LA models was simulated by solving the monodomain equation using the finite-element method.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation methodology.

claim: All simulations were executed on the Hyak supercomputer system at the University of Washington using the openCARP software package.
source: All simulations were executed on the Hyak supercomputer system at the University of Washington using the openCARP software package (Vigmond et al., 2003; Vigmond et al., 2008)
evidence: This is a description of the computational infrastructure with citations to Vigmond et al., 2003 and Vigmond et al., 2008.

claim: The compute time required to complete each unique simulation ranged from 1 to 10 hr.
source: The compute time required to complete each unique simulation ranged from 1 to 10 hr.
evidence: This is a description of the computational cost.

claim: The total CPU time for all simulations conducted in all models was 13.4 years.
source: The total CPU time for all simulations conducted in all models was 13.4 years.
evidence: This is a description of the total computational cost.

claim: Arrhythmia induction via rapid pacing was attempted from 15 pacing sites derived from AFib trigger sites.
source: Arrhythmia induction via rapid pacing was attempted from 15 pacing sites derived from AFib trigger sites (Figure 1C, see caption for detailed anatomical site descriptions) (Santangeli and Marchlinski, 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation protocol with citation to Santangeli and Marchlinski, 2017 and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: A clinically relevant pacing sequence of 12 electrical stimuli was delivered at each of the 15 locations.
source: As in previous publications, a clinically relevant pacing sequence of 12 electrical stimuli was delivered at each of the 15 locations (Zahid et al., 2016a; Zahid et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a description of the pacing protocol with citations to prior studies.

claim: Individual cell-scale ionic models were paced to limit cycle at a rate basic cycle length of 500 ms.
source: Individual cell-scale ionic models were paced to limit cycle at a rate basic cycle length of 500 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the initial conditions for the simulations.

claim: The electrical stimulus consisted of two initial pulses with a coupling interval of 300 ms, followed by pulses ramping down to 200 ms in 20 ms intervals.
source: The electrical stimulus consisted of two initial pulses with a coupling interval of 300 ms, followed by pulses ramping down to 200 ms in 20 ms intervals.
evidence: This is a description of the pacing protocol.

claim: For all cases in which activity persisted for at least 5000 ms post-pacing, further analysis was applied to determine whether the cause was an induced RD or macroscopic reentry.
source: For all cases in which activity persisted for at least 5000 ms post-pacing, we applied further analysis to determine whether the cause was an induced RD or macroscopic reentry (i.e., continuous repetitive, self-sustaining activation propagating around a non-conductive obstacle such as the mitral valve or pulmonary vein(s)), which we consider flutter-like reentry.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis protocol.

claim: Instances of macroscopic reentry were excluded from further analysis.
source: Instances of macroscopic reentry were excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis protocol.

claim: The LA was subdivided into three broad anatomical areas using standardized cutoff values in the UAC space.
source: First, the LA was subdivided into three broad anatomical areas (region 1: LA floor, 2: posterior wall; 3: anterior wall including LAA) using standardized cutoff values in the UAC space (Roney et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a description of the regional analysis methodology with citation to Roney et al., 2019a.

claim: The left and right PV areas were established using a region-growing approach such that each accounted for 15% of the total LA surface area.
source: Second, the left and right PV areas (regions 4 and 5, respectively) were established using a region-growing approach such that each accounted for 15% of the total LA surface area.
evidence: This is a description of the regional analysis methodology.

claim: A constraint equation derived by support vector machine-based classification was used to delineate pro-RD regions.
source: We used a constraint equation derived by support vector machine-based classification to delineate such pro-RD regions.
evidence: This is a description of the pro-RD tissue analysis methodology.

claim: The classification polynomial was: 0.4096 FD2 +3.28(FD)(FE) − 0.1036 FE2 – 0.7112(FD) – FE + 0.0429.
source: As in prior studies (Zahid et al., 2016a; Ali et al., 2019), the classification polynomial was as follows: 0.4096 FD2 +3.28(FD)(FE) − 0.1036 FE2 – 0.7112(FD) – FE + 0.0429.
evidence: This is a description of the classification method with citations to prior studies.

claim: All 90 models were allowed to reach a quasi-equilibrium state (1000 ms in the absence of pacing).
source: To do this, we allowed all 90 models to reach a quasi-equilibrium state (1000 ms in the absence of pacing).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis protocol for abnormal depolarization.

claim: The 95th percentile of resting Vm values across all models was identified as the threshold for delineation of fibrosis-induced abnormal depolarization (–75.3 mV).
source: We aggregated resting Vm values across all models and identified the 95th percentile as the threshold for delineation of fibrosis-induced abnormal depolarization (–75.3 mV).
evidence: This is a description of the threshold determination for abnormal depolarization.

claim: Continuous variables were compared pairwise between groups using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and were reported as mean ± standard deviation.
source: Continuous variables were compared pairwise between groups using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and were reported as mean ± standard deviation.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods.

claim: Categorical variables were compared using a χ2 test.
source: Categorical variables were compared using a χ2 test.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods.

claim: Statistical significance was established at two-tailed p≤0.05.
source: Statistical significance was established at two-tailed p≤0.05.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical significance threshold.

claim: All statistical analysis was performed using R.
source: All statistical analysis was performed using R (R Development Core Team, 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical software used.
